author: A Robot
objectives: Represent 2D vectors using both magnitude/direction and x/y components.
Add vectors graphically via tip-to-tail and identify the resultant; relate to order-independence.
Decompose a vector into x- and y- (and z in the abstraction) components as reversed addition; connect to right-triangle/trig relationships.
Apply decomposition to 2D projectile motion: show independent horizontal (constant) and vertical (uniformly accelerated) motions.
Explain how vertical velocity becomes zero at maximum height and how this relates to the trajectory shape.
Predict and verify how launch angle and speed affect range and maximum height, including the 45° maximum-range result (for level ground, neglecting air resistance).
Solve and interpret a targeting challenge using projectile range predictions, and consolidate understanding in a free-exploration sandbox.
Summarize the six concept areas using guided recap.

modules.description: Students observe a single 3D vector arrow with live magnitude and direction readouts, verifying that the arrow’s definition is independent of viewpoint.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Distinguish scalar quantity from vector quantity (magnitude + direction).
Identify vector magnitude as the arrow length.
Relate vector direction to changes in the arrow’s orientation in 3D space.
Verify that magnitude/direction of the vector are intrinsic to the object, not dependent on observer viewpoint.
instructions: Move around to view the vector from different angles.
Grab the arrow head and drag to change the vector’s direction.
Watch the magnitude and direction labels update in real time.

clips.changeMeaning: Initial staging: a single visible vector arrow appears centered in the 3 m workspace, along with magnitude and direction text labels and colored reference axes so students have a fixed coordinate context for interpreting direction.
clips.narration: Vectors are quantities with both magnitude (how long) and direction (which way). Let’s explore one vector in 3D—move your viewpoint, then drag the arrow head to change it.

clips.changeMeaning: During interaction, the magnitude and direction labels switch to live-updating readouts tied to the arrow’s current orientation and length; the arrow head becomes draggable to demonstrate that the vector’s properties change with direction, not with viewpoint.
clips.narration: Drag the arrow head. As you rotate the arrow, the magnitude and the directional angles update instantly—because those describe the vector itself.

clips.changeMeaning: This clip reinforces intrinsic properties: the arrow remains steady while the labels momentarily emphasize that their values stay consistent even if students change viewing position around the object.
clips.narration: Now rotate around it. Notice: the arrow doesn’t change—only how it looks from where you stand. The vector’s magnitude and direction are defined by the arrow itself.
